conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you navigate new motherhood. Over the next few minutes I’d like to walk through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. This is a short, 10-question check-in that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past week. It helps us spot anything from the baby blues all the way to something more significant like depression or anxiety, so we can make sure you get whatever extra care or resources you might need.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words; I’ll jot down what you say.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that been hard to come by?

It’s been… pretty hard, honestly. I still get little sparks—like when my husband sends me a funny video or when the baby gives me that gummy smile—but the big, bright excitement I used to feel for things I love, like brunch with friends or even just a quiet coffee alone, feels dimmed. Mostly I’m going through the motions because I know I “should” enjoy them, but the joy part feels kind of muffled.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like, my husband made this dumb joke about diaper explosions the other night and I actually giggled—but it feels kind of forced, you know? It’s not that easy, natural laugh I used to have. Most of the time it’s like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really find things funny, even when I know they’re supposed to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself, “Tomorrow I’ll feel excited about our walk to the park or that show I used to binge,” but when the moment comes it’s flat—like someone let the air out of it. I still plan stuff, hoping the spark will come back, but mostly I’m just relieved when the day is over.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that one hits. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong—probably my milk isn’t enough or I missed his sleepy cue.” Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or forgetting to pack a burp cloth, turns into this loop of “I’m a terrible mom.” I know logically it’s not all on me, but the guilt still shows up way more than it should.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly picture him not breathing, or I’ll worry the car seat isn’t clicked in right even though I already triple-checked it. It’s like my mind refuses to stop scanning for danger. Sometimes I can take a breath and talk myself down, but the thoughts keep circling back.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, a couple of times this week. Once, about two nights ago, I was just folding laundry while the baby napped and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get a full breath. Nothing triggered it—I wasn’t even thinking about anything scary—but for a few minutes I honestly wondered if I was having a heart attack. It passed after I paced the hallway and did the breathing trick the nurse showed me, but it left me shaky the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like I’m treading water: the second I finish feeding him, there’s laundry or bottles or texts I haven’t answered, and I never quite feel on top of it. I get through the basics, but it’s exhausting and I end the day thinking, “I barely kept us afloat.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I just lay there after the baby’s last feed, staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy knot of sadness and “what-ifs.” My mind keeps replaying everything I might have messed up, and even when I’m exhausted I can’t drift off. I probably fall asleep an hour or two later than I want, then wake up again with my heart pounding over some random worry.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most days this week. It’s not crying-all-day awful, just this steady gray feeling—like I’m walking around under a cloud. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel tears behind my eyes for no real reason. It lifts a little if someone visits or the baby smiles, but the sad heaviness keeps sliding back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice in the past week it got that bad. Once was after I couldn’t get him settled for, like, an hour—he kept rooting but wouldn’t latch—and I just sat in the glider with tears rolling down while he cried on my chest. The other time was yesterday morning; I spilled the freshly pumped milk and the frustration piled onto everything else and I broke down right there in the kitchen.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It has… just quick flashes, maybe once or twice. I’ll be standing at the top of the stairs holding the baby and think, “What if I just dropped us both?” Then I hug him tighter and the thought scares me. I don’t want to die and I don’t have a plan—I just want the pressure and sadness to stop for a minute.

I hear how heavy these early weeks have felt-how the joy you expected still feels distant and gray, how even little laughs seem forced, and how the constant worries about your baby's safety leave you exhausted and on edge. You're working so hard to keep everything afloat, yet the sadness, tearfulness, and scary thoughts keep creeping in.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports laughing only rarely and describes it as forced, indicating a clear reduction from her usual enjoyment.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure—plans feel flat and she is relieved when the day ends—matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states she blames herself "way more than it should" and gives multiple examples of frequent, pervasive self-blame.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries with vivid catastrophic images and persistent scanning for danger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness) occurring multiple times, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports "most days" feeling overwhelmed and describes persistent struggle to keep up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of sleep difficulty directly linked to unhappiness and racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness "most days this week" with tearfulness and pervasive "gray" mood, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific, intrusive self-harm thoughts occurring occasionally, matching "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 23 meets the EPDS threshold for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset; core symptoms include <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> without plan. These patterns align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full risk and safety evaluation
2. Complete safety plan including 24/7 support person and removal of potential hazards
3. Consider initiation of evidence-based therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and discuss antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding
4. Schedule EPDS re-screen within one week to track response
5. Provide crisis resources: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, local 24-hour hotline, and emergency department if thoughts escalate
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Plus supplemental inquiry, self-report, 2 wks post-delivery

Identified Symptoms / Behaviors  
- Persistent low mood, described as “steady gray feeling,” present most days  
- Marked anhedonia: planned activities feel “flat,” laughter described as forced  
- Daily excessive guilt / self-blame (“terrible mom” cognitions)  
- Recurrent intrusive worries (infant safety, car seat, etc.)  
- Two episodes of sudden panic (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to rumination and “what-ifs”  
- Frequent tearfulness; two tearful breakdowns in past week  
- Sense of being overwhelmed / “treading water” with daily tasks  
- Passive self-harm ideation (flashes of dropping infant and self down stairs), no intent or plan

Pattern Summary  
Across domains: mood, anxiety, coping, and safety. Symptoms present >50% of days, interfere with sleep and functioning. No psychotic features reported; appetite/weight inquiry not assessed.

Screening Significance / Risk Flags  
1. Meets screening threshold for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset  
2. Co-occurring anxiety symptoms consistent with peripartum generalized/panic spectrum  
3. Safety concern: presence of passive suicidal/harm ideation (requires immediate risk assessment)

Next Step  
Urgent follow-up appointment scheduled for full risk evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options.
